strengths: Introduces a well-motivated intermediate tokenization strategy (2D cortical flat maps) that preserves full-resolution fMRI signal while enabling direct reuse of standard, well-optimized ViT/video-MAE machinery, positioned sensibly between lossy parcellation approaches and computationally expensive native 4D volumetric approaches.

Large-scale, carefully documented pretraining (2.3K hours from HCP, 8.2M frames) with clear preprocessing pipeline (flat map construction via pycortex, background-patch exclusion) and thorough implementation details in the appendix, aiding reproducibility.

Reports what the authors claim is the first clean power-law scaling relationship between fMRI masked-reconstruction loss and pretraining dataset size, an interesting empirical observation relevant to the fMRI foundation-model community.

Introduces a novel and creative downstream benchmark (NSD CLIP global-label classification) that tests zero-shot cross-subject generalization to an out-of-distribution dataset and stimulus type not seen in pretraining.

Competitive downstream performance (HCP state decoding, UKBB sex classification) relative to prior specialized methods despite using much shorter input clips (16s) and a frozen encoder with only a shallow probe trained on a small subset of target-domain data.

Transparent, honest reporting of negative/mixed findings (e.g., non-monotonic scaling of downstream performance with data and model size, weaker OOD scaling, ViT-L underperforming ViT-B), which strengthens scientific credibility even though it tempers the paper's central scaling-law narrative.
weaknesses: The central 'strict power law' scaling claim is derived from only 5 dataset-size points spanning less than one order of magnitude (0.5M-7.4M frames) using a single architecture (ViT-B); this is a fairly narrow empirical base to support such a strong and prominently advertised claim, and no error bars, repeated runs, or statistical tests accompany the fit.

The scaling law does not translate into consistently improved downstream task performance: results are explicitly non-monotonic across dataset size and model size, and the largest model (ViT-L) performs worse than much smaller models, undermining the practical significance of the reported scaling behavior and suggesting possible optimization/hyperparameter confounds that are not investigated.

No controlled, apples-to-apples comparison against alternative tokenization strategies (parcellation-based or native 4D volumetric models) trained under the same data/compute budget; the two included baselines (connectome, patch embedding) are simple and not full re-implementations of competing published architectures, so the core claim that flat maps are a superior representation is not rigorously demonstrated.

Comparisons to prior state-of-the-art (Brain-JEPA, BrainLM, NeuroSTORM, Thomas et al.) are acknowledged by the authors themselves to be apples-to-oranges (different pretraining data, clip lengths, fine-tuning vs. frozen-encoder protocols, class counts), making the claimed near-state-of-the-art / near-ceiling results difficult to interpret as genuine evidence of superiority.

The model is pretrained solely on HCP; the weaker/saturating scaling behavior on the OOD NSD set is interpreted by the authors as a sign of insufficient data diversity, which is a reasonable but unresolved limitation that constrains the paper's 'foundation model' framing.

The new NSD CLIP benchmark, while creative, uses an ad hoc, potentially ill-posed labeling scheme (single global CLIP-assigned label for complex multi-object scenes) and yields low absolute accuracies (14-21%), making it unclear how meaningful or reproducible this benchmark is as a community evaluation tool.

Downstream results are reported as single numbers without multiple seeds, confidence intervals, or significance testing, limiting the ability to assess whether observed differences (e.g., across dataset/model size sweeps) are statistically meaningful versus noise.

The paper explicitly self-identifies as 'work in progress' with several core comparisons (to volumetric/parcellation baselines, alternative SSL objectives) deferred to future work, and the code/dataset link is not provided in the current version, which raises reproducibility concerns for evaluating the submission as it stands.

strengths: The flat-map tokenization strategy is a reasonable and well-motivated middle ground between heavily lossy ROI-parcellation approaches and computationally expensive native 4D volumetric modeling; it allows a standard ViT/MAE pipeline to be applied with minimal architectural modification.

The empirical design is fairly thorough for a first study: the paper systematically ablates pretraining dataset size, model size, and temporal patch size, and evaluates on three distinct downstream tasks (HCP state decoding, UKBB sex classification, and a newly constructed NSD CLIP-label decoding benchmark) spanning in- and out-of-distribution settings.

Masked reconstruction visualizations (Fig. 2, Fig. 8) and the denoising interpretation of MAE are a nice qualitative sanity check that the model is learning spatially coherent structure rather than memorizing noise.

The paper is transparent about its preliminary status and explicitly discusses the mismatch between the clean power-law scaling of pretraining loss and the much weaker/non-monotonic scaling of downstream decoding performance, rather than overselling the result.
Appendices provide reasonable implementation detail (flat-map construction pipeline, pretraining hyperparameters, probe protocol, benchmark construction) that aids reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central claimed contribution -- a 'strict power scaling law' for masked reconstruction loss -- is not shown to translate into any practically meaningful scaling benefit: downstream decoding performance vs. data size is explicitly reported as non-monotonic and weak (Fig. 4, left column), undermining the paper's framing of this as 'a hallmark of an effective foundation model.' The scaling-law evidence itself rests on only 5 dataset-size points and a 3-point fit for the OOD curve, which is a thin basis for the strong claims made in the abstract/intro.

Model-size scaling results are counter to typical foundation-model expectations (ViT-L underperforms a much smaller 12.4M-parameter model) and this anomaly is noted but not investigated or explained, leaving open whether it reflects overfitting, optimization issues, or a fundamental limit of the approach/data.

Comparisons to prior fMRI foundation models (SwiFT, BrainLM, Brain-JEPA, NeuroSTORM, Thomas et al.) are all indirect, citing numbers from different splits, label counts, sequence lengths, and fine-tuning protocols; the paper itself acknowledges 'it is not straightforward to compare... performance across prior works,' which weakens the evidentiary basis for claims of matching or approaching state of the art.

No error bars, confidence intervals, or repeated runs are reported for any of the downstream decoding results, making it hard to assess whether the differences shown in Figure 4 (e.g., across model/data/patch sizes) are statistically meaningful or within noise, especially for the smaller evaluation sets (as small as ~60K samples, sometimes with only a few hundred held-out subjects).

Pretraining relies solely on HCP, a relatively homogeneous, extensively curated research dataset; the paper acknowledges this limits diversity and likely explains the saturating OOD scaling behavior, but does not attempt mitigation or quantify how much this limits generalization claims.

The NSD CLIP classification benchmark is newly introduced by the authors, uses an arbitrary and somewhat ad hoc 41-category labeling scheme derived from unsupervised clustering with manual inspection, and has no external baseline or prior literature result for comparison, making the reported '>8x better than chance' difficult to contextualize as a meaningful contribution.

Novelty is primarily a dataset-representation choice (flat maps) combined with off-the-shelf VideoMAE/ViT architectures; the technical contribution beyond prior volumetric or parcellation-based fMRI transformers is incremental, and no direct controlled comparison (same data, same splits) against parcellation-based or native 4D baselines is provided to isolate the benefit of flat maps specifically.

The paper explicitly self-identifies as 'a work in progress' and lists a long set of unresolved future directions (diversity of pretraining data, robustness of scaling claims, direct baseline comparisons, alternative SSL objectives, representation analysis, broader benchmarks), suggesting the work is not yet mature enough to support its stated conclusions at publication quality.

strengths: Introduces a conceptually clean and well-motivated intermediate tokenization strategy (cortical flat maps) that bridges the gap between lossy parcellation-based approaches and computationally expensive native 4D volumetric approaches, while preserving full spatial resolution of the fMRI signal.

Enables direct reuse of mature, standard ViT/video-MAE architectures and training recipes with only minimal modification (background-patch exclusion), which is an elegant and practical engineering contribution.

Demonstrates a clean power-law scaling relationship between pretraining dataset size and masked reconstruction loss on in-distribution data, which is a novel and noteworthy observation for the fMRI foundation model literature.
Includes a reasonably thorough set of ablations: dataset size, model size, and temporal patch size, together with two sensible simple baselines (connectome and patch-embedding) for comparison.

Introduces a new, arguably more ecologically meaningful cross-subject decoding benchmark (NSD CLIP classification) that tests out-of-distribution, zero-shot generalization to unseen subjects and an unseen dataset, with promising preliminary results.
Reasonably transparent and honest about the preliminary/exploratory nature of the work, explicitly framing it as part of an ongoing open-science effort and outlining concrete next steps.
Good methodological documentation in the appendix (flat map construction pipeline, pretraining/probe hyperparameters, benchmark construction), supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Pretraining relies solely on HCP, a relatively homogeneous dataset (healthy young adults, specific scanner/protocol); the paper itself notes that OOD scaling on NSD saturates, suggesting the strong in-distribution power law may partly reflect overfitting to HCP-specific statistics rather than generalizable representation learning.

The central scaling-law claim is based on only 5 dataset-size points and a single architecture/seed, which is a thin empirical basis for claiming a 'strict' power law; no confidence intervals, repeated runs, or sensitivity analysis are reported.

Downstream decoding results do not scale monotonically with data or model size (e.g., ViT-L underperforms smaller models, the 3.2M-frame model beats the 7.4M model on two of three benchmarks), which undercuts the practical relevance of the observed pretraining-loss scaling law and is not fully explained.

Comparisons to prior state-of-the-art methods (HCP state decoding, UKBB sex classification) are explicitly acknowledged as not well controlled (different splits, label counts, clip lengths, fine-tuning vs. frozen-probe protocols), making the claimed competitive/near-SOTA performance difficult to assess rigorously.

The NSD CLIP benchmark, while novel, uses a coarse single global label for complex multi-object scenes and is evaluated on a single held-out subject, limiting the strength of conclusions about general cross-subject zero-shot decoding.

No statistical significance testing or variance estimates (e.g., across seeds, subjects, or bootstrap resampling) are reported for any of the downstream benchmarks, making it hard to judge whether reported performance differences are meaningful.

The paper is explicitly a work-in-progress/short paper lacking some of the depth expected for a full research contribution (e.g., no direct head-to-head comparison against native 4D or parcellation-based baselines using the same pretraining data and protocol, as the authors themselves note as future work).

strengths: Introduces a novel and well-motivated intermediate 'flat map' representation for fMRI-ViT modeling that sits between lossy parcellation and computationally heavy volumetric approaches, with a clear conceptual framing (the 'goldilocks zone' hypothesis).

Extensive, carefully designed experimental suite: masked reconstruction visualizations, denoising, scaling analysis over both data and model size, and numerous ablations (masking strategy, augmentation, normalization, decoder architecture, patch size, subcortical inclusion, temporal sequence length).

Introduces BRAINMARKS, an open, reproducible benchmark suite spanning trait prediction and dynamic state decoding across 7 public datasets and 6+ prior foundation models, addressing a genuine reproducibility gap in the field (as the authors document in Table 15/6, several published models were evaluated with broken normalization, which the authors correct).

Honest reporting of null/negative results (no representation or model clearly beats a simple functional-connectivity baseline on trait prediction; unclear scaling advantage on OOD NSD data), which strengthens scientific credibility.

Interesting emergent finding that the model's learned spatial position embedding recovers the brain's default mode network/functional gradient without explicit supervision, and useful engineering ablations (e.g., cross-register decoding, edge masking) that could be broadly useful to the community.
Strong commitment to open science: code, data preprocessing (flat map construction), pretraining hyperparameters, and benchmark protocols are documented in detail, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central claim that flat maps 'generally perform best' is only partially supported: Table 2 shows volume representation wins on age prediction, parcellation is most compute-efficient, and none of the representations shows a decisive edge on the four clinical diagnosis datasets — the headline claim is therefore representation- and task-dependent rather than a general result.

Trait/diagnosis prediction results (Figure 8, Table 14) show that none of the foundation models, including the authors' own, reliably beats the simple connectome baseline, which somewhat undercuts the paper's motivating premise that foundation models bring clear value; while this is reported transparently, it limits the paper's positive contribution to state decoding only.

Scaling experiments are conducted at fairly modest scale (up to ~37M encoder parameters, single-dataset pretraining on HCP-YA up to ~2K hours), so the reported power laws and 'hard limit on model size' claims may not generalize to the scale regimes typical of foundation-model scaling studies in vision/language; the weaker scaling exponent versus language models is noted but not deeply investigated.

Cross-model comparisons in BRAINMARKS (Section 5.4) combine architecture, pretraining data, representation, and objective differences across baselines (SwiFT, BrainLM, Brain-JEPA, NeuroSTORM, etc.), making it difficult to cleanly attribute performance differences to representation choice versus other confounding design decisions.

Generalization to out-of-distribution data (NSD) is comparatively weak and scaling improvements saturate faster than in-distribution HCP-YA, and the UKBB pretraining experiment (Appendix C.2) surprisingly underperforms HCP-YA pretraining even with 10x more data, raising questions about how robust the scaling/representation conclusions are outside the primary pretraining source.

Considerable amount of critical methodological detail and several key results (e.g., normalization ablations, compute comparisons, coordinate-norm effects) are relegated to the appendix, making the main text somewhat difficult to fully assess without cross-referencing extensive supplementary material.

The ethics/limitations discussion is brief; deeper discussion of clinical translation risks or dataset demographic biases (e.g., HCP-YA being a young, likely non-representative population) is largely absent.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely useful and underexplored intermediate fMRI representation (cortical flat maps) that lets a standard ViT/MAE pipeline be applied to fMRI with minimal architectural change, filling a real gap between lossy parcellation and computationally heavy dense volume representations.

Provides the first open, reproducible benchmark suite (BRAINMARKS) spanning 7 public datasets and both trait-prediction and dynamic-state-decoding tasks, with a carefully documented, controlled evaluation protocol (linear probes, attentive probes, dense learning-rate grids, matched compute), which is a valuable community contribution independent of the specific model.

Extensive and honest ablation program (masking strategy, data augmentation, reconstruction target/patch normalization, temporal/spatial patch size, subcortical structures, input normalization, decoder architecture, sequence length, pretraining data mixture, scale) covering >15 tables/figures, with results reported even when they are negative or inconclusive (e.g., no benefit from common vision augmentations, no scaling benefit from more diverse UKBB data, unreliable trait-prediction gains over an FC baseline).

Careful and transparent scaling-law analysis for both data and model size, explicitly contrasting in-distribution vs out-of-distribution generalization and reporting a weaker/saturating exponent than language-model scaling rather than overclaiming.

Good methodological hygiene: normalization ablations reveal that several prior fMRI foundation models were evaluated without coordinate normalization, causing near-chance performance, and the authors correct for this in their comparisons — a useful diagnostic contribution to the field.
Open, reproducible codebase and 100% open pretraining data (HCP-YA), aligning with stated open-science goals.
weaknesses: The central empirical claims are mixed and often null: no representation (parcel/flat/volume) is uniformly best, no foundation model reliably beats a simple functional-connectivity baseline on four of six trait-prediction datasets, and attentive vs. logistic probe rankings are within each other's confidence intervals — this substantially limits the paper's significance as a demonstration that self-supervised fMRI foundation models provide a clear advance over simple baselines.

The scaling-law finding is qualified as "strict" only in-distribution (HCP-YA) and explicitly breaks down / saturates out-of-distribution (NSD) and with more diverse data (UKBB), and downstream probe performance saturates at a relatively small model size (~37M encoder params); this undercuts the paper's title framing around 'scaling' as a strong, generalizable result.

The core architectural contribution (patch-embedding a ViT on flattened cortical surface maps) is an incremental engineering adaptation of an existing method (MAE-st) to a new but conceptually straightforward 2D representation, rather than a new learning method or theoretical insight; novelty is largely in application/representation choice.

Pretraining relies on a single source dataset (HCP-YA, healthy young adults 22-35), and the paper's own experiment shows UKBB pretraining underperforms HCP-YA even with 10x more data, raising concerns about generalizability of the trained CortexMAE models to more diverse or clinical populations relevant to the diagnosis-focused trait benchmarks.

Trait prediction results on clinical diagnosis datasets (ABIDE, ADHD-200, ADNI, PPMI) are reported as unreliable/noisy across all models including the proposed one, meaning the paper's most clinically relevant benchmarks yield a genuine null result for the entire field, not just competitors — this is honestly reported but weakens the practical impact case.

Some ablations (e.g., cross-register decoding, decoder edge masking, PC-norm reconstruction targets) are interesting but only marginally improve or fail to clearly improve performance, and are relegated to appendices without strong takeaways, diluting the paper's focus.
The flat map projection is lossy for subcortical structures and the paper acknowledges it cannot represent ~15% of gray matter, a nontrivial limitation for a claimed general fMRI representation.

Comparisons to prior foundation models (BrainLM, Brain-JEPA, SwiFT, NeuroSTORM, etc.) depend heavily on reproducing/re-evaluating them under the authors' own normalization and probing protocol, which, while well-motivated, means some conclusions about prior work's poor performance rest on the authors' own reimplementation choices rather than the original papers' reported settings.

strengths: Introduces a novel and well-motivated intermediate fMRI representation (cortical flat maps) that sits between lossy parcellation and expensive dense volume representations, and shows this 'goldilocks' representation is compatible directly with standard ViT patch embeddings without architectural modification.

Provides a genuinely useful community resource: BRAINMARKS, an open, reproducible benchmark suite spanning seven datasets and both trait-prediction and dynamic state-decoding tasks, addressing a well-documented reproducibility gap in the fMRI foundation model literature (as the authors cite via Pineau et al., 2021).

Conducts the first systematic scaling-law analysis for fMRI masked reconstruction (both data and model size), reporting power-law fits and honestly noting the limits of scaling (saturation, weak OOD generalization), which is a valuable empirical contribution even though results are modest in absolute terms.

Extensive, well-designed ablations (masking strategy, augmentation, reconstruction target, patch size, subcortical structures, input normalization, decoder architecture, edge-masking) that go beyond a single headline result and meaningfully inform future fMRI modeling choices, e.g., the striking finding that coordinate normalization is essential for state decoding performance.

Honest and non-cherry-picked reporting: the paper explicitly reports a 'null result' that no single model reliably beats a simple functional-connectivity baseline on trait prediction, and discusses this transparently rather than overstating results, which strengthens scientific credibility.

Strong reproducibility commitment: open code/models/data, detailed hyperparameter tables, dense learning-rate grids for fair probe tuning across models, and an described fully transparent, discord-based open-research development process.

Interesting emergent-property finding that the model's learned spatial position embedding recovers the brain's default mode network / principal gradient without explicit supervision, adding some interpretability value.
weaknesses: The central empirical claims are mixed: while flat maps win on state decoding, volume representation wins on age prediction and parcellation is best on trait prediction/compute efficiency, so the 'goldilocks representation' framing is not uniformly supported by the results, and the paper acknowledges this itself ('flat maps do not universally outperform the alternatives').

Trait prediction results are described as unreliable/inconsistent across all models including the proposed one, and no model reliably beats a simple FC connectome baseline—this substantially weakens the practical significance of the proposed foundation model family for one of the two main application areas studied.

Scaling analysis is conducted on a single pretraining source (HCP-YA) and a single architecture family, limiting generalizability of the reported power-law exponents; the UKBB scaling experiment (Appendix C.2) surprisingly shows worse performance than HCP-YA even with 10x more data, which is only briefly discussed as 'preliminary' without deeper investigation of why the scaling law breaks down.

The comparison against prior models (SwiFT, BrainLM, Brain-JEPA, NeuroSTORM, BrainHarmonix-F, Brain-Semantoks) may be affected by uneven pretraining/preprocessing normalization choices, as shown by Table 6/15 where coordinate normalization dramatically changes performance; although the authors control for this at evaluation time, it raises questions about whether the baseline comparisons fully reflect each model's original design intent versus retrofitted evaluation protocol.

Model scale explored (up to ~37M encoder parameters, ViT-B scale) is small relative to modern vision/language foundation models, so claims about 'scaling' are limited to a narrow regime; the paper is transparent about this limit but it still constrains how much the scaling-law claims generalize.

Clinical/diagnostic sample sizes (400-900 subjects) are inherently small, and the paper itself notes no reliable differences between representations on these datasets, which somewhat undercuts the diagnostic-relevance motivation raised in the introduction and impact statement.
